idiom_name: com.sun.source TreeScanner and TreePathScanner with Trees (read-only), TreeTranslator inside javac
implementation_notes: The supported route is com.sun.source: parse with JavacTask or Trees, override visitBinary and the other visitX methods of TreeScanner, and use TreePathScanner when a rule needs the enclosing path because the shape alone does not identify the site (getCurrentPath carries the parent chain). Matching is a kind check plus a cast (node.getKind() == Tree.Kind.PLUS, ((LiteralTree) node.getRightOperand()).getValue()), so the pattern is Java code, not data. The API is read-only by design, so a rewrite pass must either collect text edits at node positions or rebuild nodes; javac itself uses com.sun.tools.javac.tree.TreeTranslator, whose javadoc states it is not a supported API. Pattern matching for switch over sealed record hierarchies (Java 21) is the light-weight path when the tree is your own type hierarchy rather than a JDK tree.
pitfalls: com.sun.source has no node replacement, so a rewrite must be text edits or javac internals; mixing the two produces stale source positions and edits that do not apply.
A TreeScanner must be started with scan(TreePath, P) to maintain the path; starting from scan(Tree, P) leaves getCurrentPath() empty for any rule that depends on the parent chain.
com.sun.tools.javac.tree.TreeTranslator operates on JCTree and is explicitly unsupported, so a rule built on it breaks across JDK upgrades and needs --add-exports to run at all.

variants.name: ANTLR parse tree patterns (compileParseTreePattern)
variants.idiom_name: ParseTreePattern with compileParseTreePattern, tags and labels over an ANTLR parse tree
variants.implementation_notes: When the tree is an ANTLR parse tree - the realization Parr's book presents - the pattern is written as source in the notation of one rule: tags such as <ID> and <expr> stand for any token or subtree, labels name the parts you want back, and parser.compileParseTreePattern(pattern, MyParser.RULE_x) compiles it once. match tests a single subtree and findAll walks for matches (optionally restricted by an XPath expression that selects candidate roots), each returning a ParseTreeMatch whose get and getAll expose the bound nodes by label; getPatternTree builds a tree from a partial input fragment. Rewriting means rebuilding a replacement tree or applying token edits. This is the closest thing to a declarative rule table in Java and the only variant here that needs no compiler internals.
pitfalls: A pattern is compiled against exactly one rule, so a shape that can occur under several rules needs one pattern per rule or an XPath pre-filter; a mismatched rule throws at compile time, not at match time.

Tags match any token or subtree, so <ID> can also match structural nodes; rules that must be precise need labels plus explicit checks on the captured tree, and a wrong label is only noticed when the capture is used.
A parse tree has no semantic model: scope, resolution and types are invisible to the pattern, so semantic conditions need a separate symbol-table pass.
